topics.title: Pattern overview
topics.summary: Put the rules for collaboration in one mediator so peer components do not need to know and call each other. Worked example: A form with one readiness policy. Form owns its controls and implements a small Events interface. The field reports changes, the mediator reads all relevant state, and the button updates silently.

blocks.title: Learning objectives
items: Move cross-component rules into one coordinator.
Trace events and silent state updates without a feedback loop.
Distinguish owned child components from borrowed coordinator references.

blocks.text: A component completes its local change and notifies a mediator. The mediator interprets the event in the wider context, then calls the components that must react. This central policy replaces peer-to-peer coordination. It does not mean every class belongs in one giant controller; a mediator should cover one coherent collaboration with clear event rules.

cards.question: What problem does Mediator address?
cards.answer: Put the rules for collaboration in one mediator so peer components do not need to know and call each other. Worked example: A form with one readiness policy. Form owns its controls and implements a small Events interface. The field reports changes, the mediator reads all relevant state, and the button updates silently.

cards.question: What is Mediator?
cards.answer: An object that owns rules for how other components work together.

cards.question: What is Callback?
cards.answer: A function call made back to code supplied or represented by another object.

cards.question: What is Silent update?
cards.answer: A state change that deliberately sends no new change event.

cards.question: What is Feedback loop?
cards.answer: A chain of events that returns to its starting point and may repeat.

cards.question: Why does the supplied DoC notification not keep calling DoC forever?
cards.answer: Notify reacts only to A and D. The C notification reaches no branch and returns.

cards.question: Should NameField learn whether consent was accepted?
cards.answer: No. That would put the shared readiness rule back into a reusable component. It reports its change; Form combines the relevant state.

cards.question: Why does NameField report a change instead of directly enabling SaveButton?
cards.answer: The field knows its value but not the complete form policy. Form combines name, consent and hold in one place, preventing inconsistent partial decisions.

cards.question: Why are silent button updates important?
cards.answer: If enabling the button emitted another change that repeated coordination, it could form a feedback loop. The mediator updates derived state without recursively notifying itself.

cards.question: Does an unchanged name need another event here?
cards.answer: No. NameField checks equality first. The current value has not changed, so the form does not need a redundant recomputation for that input.

cards.question: What invariant should a table-driven test cover?
cards.answer: For all combinations, enabled equals nonempty name AND accepted consent AND no hold. Testing the truth table catches accidentally dropped conditions.

cards.question: Could Form become too large as fields grow?
cards.answer: Yes. A mediator reduces links among controls but can collect too much policy. Split independent coordination responsibilities when they no longer belong to one coherent form rule.

cards.question: Why is copying Form forbidden?
cards.answer: NameField stores a reference to its mediator. A naive copy could leave the copied field reporting to the original form instead of its new owner.

cards.question: When would direct field interaction be simpler?
cards.answer: For two controls with one stable rule and no growing web of dependencies. Central coordination becomes valuable as several inputs jointly determine behavior.

topics.title: The problem: one form rule spreads across several controls
topics.summary: A save form has a name field, a consent choice, and a save button. The button should be enabled only when the name is nonempty and consent is accepted. An attempted save while disabled must return false and leave the save count unchanged. Start with one function that computes the rule. If the program is just a small procedural form, that single function is enough. The need for a new structure appears when reusable field and button components must participate without learning the private details of one another.

blocks.text: One tempting design gives the name field a button pointer and has it enable the button whenever text appears. Then the consent control also changes the button. The two controls now need to know the same combined rule. If the name field enables the button without checking consent, typing a name bypasses the requirement. If both controls know each other, changes to the form ripple through all of them. We need one owner of the collaboration rule while keeping the controls responsible for their own simple behavior.

topics.title: Let components report; let the form decide
topics.summary: A mediator is an object that coordinates the interaction of other objects. Here Form is the mediator. NameField stores text and reports a changed event. SaveButton stores whether it is enabled. Neither component needs to call the other. Form knows the rule that combines a filled name with accepted consent, so its changed function recomputes the button state from current facts.

blocks.text: The small Events interface lets NameField report a change without depending on the concrete Form class. The field receives Events& in its constructor: a required borrowed relationship with no null state. Events has a virtual destructor and a pure virtual changed function. Form implements changed using override, so a misspelled or incompatible replacement is caught during compilation. This interface is justified by reusing the same field with another coordinator. If the form had no reusable components, a direct helper function would be simpler.

topics.title: Follow one change from input to visible state
topics.summary: Form::name takes a string by value and moves it into NameField::set. The move permits the string storage to be transferred instead of copied when possible; it does not turn the string into a raw pointer. set compares the new text with the old text. Equal text returns immediately because it creates no new fact for the coordinator. Otherwise the field stores the new value and then calls events_.changed. That order matters: the mediator must observe the updated field, not yesterday’s text.

blocks.text: changed reads name_.filled, combines that result with accepted_ using &&, and calls save_.enable. Logical AND is true only when both conditions are true. The local ready value means the name condition alone; the final expression still checks consent. The button update is silent: enable stores a bool but does not report another event. The event direction therefore ends after one coordination step. A mediator is not a promise that loops cannot occur; these particular method contracts are what prevent a feedback loop.

topics.title: Ownership and callbacks must fit together
topics.summary: Form contains NameField and SaveButton by value, so it owns their lifetimes. Its constructor initializes name_ with *this, a reference to the Form being constructed, treated as its Events base. Passing this reference during construction is safe here because the NameField constructor only stores it and does not call changed. Calling back before all Form members had been initialized would make the coordinator read incomplete state. The code deliberately has no such constructor callback.

blocks.text: The field borrows the mediator it lives inside. This creates a relationship cycle in the object graph, but not an ownership cycle: only Form owns the field; the field does not own Form. Copy and assignment are deleted, which also prevents an implicit move constructor in this design. Without that restriction, a default copy of the field reference would still refer to the original Form, and changes in the copied form could update the wrong button. A more flexible movable form would need to rebind every callback relationship during its move operation.

topics.title: The coordinator owns policy, not every job
topics.summary: Form::submit checks the current button state and returns false if saving is disabled. The successful path increments saved_, a small local stand-in for completed saves in this demonstration. It does not write a file, send a request, or claim durability. The tests use the count to prove that rejected submissions had no effect. In a real form, the save service belongs behind a separate interface; the mediator can call it, but should not absorb file formats, storage retries, and every other subsystem rule.

blocks.text: Consent changes go through accept, which stores the new bool and calls changed. A repeated accept may recompute the button even if nothing changed; recomputing this pure boolean rule is harmless. The name field avoids equal-text notifications to demonstrate a useful event contract. Neither behavior is inherently more correct. What matters is that listeners know whether setters always notify, notify only on actual change, or never notify. Naming and tests should make the policy visible rather than leave users to infer it from a framework.

topics.title: Control the growth of the mediator
topics.summary: When forms gain dozens of unrelated behaviors, the mediator can become one huge object that knows too much. Divide coordination by purpose: a validation controller can decide readiness, a storage service can save, and a page controller can choose which view is shown. The goal is a clear home for a specific collaboration, not one central object for an entire application. Do not make every event a string if a small typed interface can keep mistakes visible to the compiler.

blocks.text: The lab adds a temporary hold flag. A held form must disable save even with valid text and consent; lifting the hold must recompute from the other conditions. This change belongs in the mediator because neither the field nor the button knows what a hold means. The extension tests preserve both old rejection cases and the save count. The same reasoning is useful in an editor, setup wizard, or simulation control panel: components announce local changes, and a coordinator decides what those changes mean together.

blocks.title: Requirements
items: Enable save only for a nonempty name with accepted consent.

blocks.title: Invariants
items: Button readiness equals filled name AND accepted consent after each public change.
Disabled submit leaves the saved count unchanged.
A field callback always reaches its containing live Form.
Button enable does not emit a new changed event.

blocks.text: Alternative: A single procedural update_ready function is sufficient for a form with no reusable controls. Letting each control directly alter every peer can look shorter initially but duplicates the combined rule and creates fragile dependencies.

It exercises only local synchronous coordination and a small count; it does not test storage, thread safety, or unlimited-count overflow.

topics.title: Exercise 16.6: Justify a decision
topics.summary: Explain why a borrowed field-to-Form reference is acceptable even though the relationship graph contains a cycle.

blocks.title: Hint
blocks.text: Separate relationships from ownership.

blocks.title: Explained answer
blocks.text: Form owns its field by value; the field only borrows Form. There is no shared ownership cycle to keep both alive forever. Construction and destruction rules still must ensure the borrowed reference is used only while Form is valid.

workshop.title: A form with one readiness policy
workshop.problem: A form with one readiness policy. Enable save only for a nonempty name with accepted consent. Reject disabled submission without changing the saved count. Keep field and button types independent of one another.

steps.why: The default member values satisfy the readiness rule.
The name is filled, but false consent keeps save disabled.
Both conditions now hold; submit increases the count to one.
The event sees the newly empty field and disables save.

steps.state: Restoring Mina then revoking consent: enabled=false.
steps.why: Every relevant change recomputes the same combined rule.

workshop.pitfall: NameField enables save whenever text is nonempty. Entering Mina can enable save while consent is false. One component cannot decide a rule that also depends on another state.

discussion.question: Choose a mediator or direct function for a command-line prompt with two local values and no reusable controls.
discussion.answer: A direct function evaluating the two local values is clearer. Introduce a mediator only when independent components need coordinated rules or event handling that would otherwise spread between them.
discussion.hint: Do not invent peer objects without a requirement.

workshop.alternative: A single procedural update_ready function is sufficient for a form with no reusable controls. Letting each control directly alter every peer can look shorter initially but duplicates the combined rule and creates fragile dependencies.
workshop.design: Form owns its controls and implements a small Events interface. The field reports changes, the mediator reads all relevant state, and the button updates silently.
invariants: Button readiness equals filled name AND accepted consent after each public change.
Disabled submit leaves the saved count unchanged.
A field callback always reaches its containing live Form.
Button enable does not emit a new changed event.
workshop.maintenance: A new condition changes one readiness policy. Review construction, copy/move behavior, and notification contracts whenever components gain callbacks or the form becomes dynamically owned.
workshop.verification: The program checks initial rejection, name-only rejection, enabled save, unchanged input, clearing a name, revoked consent, and preserved saved count. It exercises only local synchronous coordination and a small count; it does not test storage, thread safety, or unlimited-count overflow.

focus.where: It runs when Form forwards new input to its NameField.
